analysis.one_liner: Directly approves the Keystone XL oil pipeline, bypassing normal presidential permits and further environmental review.
analysis.headline: Backed by 45 of 100 senators, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar one day after introduction but never came to a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written federal law approving the Keystone XL pipeline for TransCanada, removing the need for the presidential border permit normally required for a cross-border pipeline and declaring that no new environmental impact statement was needed. It would have treated the State Department's 2011 environmental review as satisfying every environmental law requiring federal consultation, limited all court challenges to a single appeals court in Washington, and let Nebraska's chosen route replace the contested original one.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. would be the direct beneficiary: it would receive statutory approval to build and operate the pipeline under its 2008 application, with no presidential permit required and no additional environmental impact statement [S2][S3]. Canadian oil sands producers would gain a dedicated route to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, and supporters argued the construction would create jobs (the bill text and summary themselves do not quantify jobs). Gulf Coast refiners would gain access to heavy Canadian crude.
analysis.who_benefits_short: TransCanada and Canadian oil sands producers

how_it_helps.text: Grants TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. direct congressional authorization to build, connect, operate, and maintain the cross-border pipeline facilities at Phillips County, Montana, under its September 2008 application — no presidential border permit required

Declares that no additional environmental impact statement shall be required, and deems the State Department's August 26, 2011 environmental impact statement to satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act and any other law requiring federal agency consultation or review
Provides that any action taken to implement the Act is not a 'major federal action' under NEPA, closing off a common route for legal challenges
Channels all federal judicial review of the project and related permits solely to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, instead of letting challengers file in courts along the route
Keeps already-issued federal permits in effect and lets any Nebraska-designated route supersede the original one, removing two sources of delay

analysis.who_pays: The bill would shift the cost of speed onto the review process itself: communities and landowners along the route would lose the leverage of a full, adversarial permitting process, since the bill bars any new environmental impact statement and deems the 2011 review sufficient for all environmental laws [S2][S3]. Federal and state agencies would lose their normal consultative role, and anyone harmed by the pipeline could challenge it only in the D.C. Circuit [S2][S3]. The bill itself concedes the route problem was unresolved — no construction in Nebraska could begin until the state submitted a route, and extra measures applied if it crossed the Sand Hills region [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Landowners and water resources along the route

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the presidential border permit and bars any additional environmental impact statement, cutting the public out of the review process that normally governs cross-border pipelines

It treats a single 2011 State Department review as satisfying NEPA and every other federal consultation law, even though the Nebraska route was still unresolved — construction in that state could not start until Nebraska submitted a new route, and the bill's own conditions flag special measures if it crossed the Sand Hills
It restricts all court challenges to the D.C. Circuit alone, making it harder and more expensive for affected landowners and communities to contest the project
It is legislation tailored to one named company and one named project, written around TransCanada's specific 2008 application, rather than a general rule

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For TransCanada and oil sands shippers, the bill offered speed and near-total legal certainty — approval by statute, no permit, no new review, one friendly court venue. The cost fell on the integrity of the review process: the environmental safeguards it cites (mitigation plans, safety conditions, Nebraska route stipulations) were all products of the very permitting and review machinery the bill would sidestep, and future problems could only be litigated in a single court. Even sympathetically, this is a shortcut whose main deliverable is exemption from process.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with 45 cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar the next day, but no committee acted and the Senate never voted on it before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John Hoeven introduced the bill on January 30, 2012, with 45 cosponsors — 43 Republicans and 2 Democrats — including the Republican and Democratic leadership ranks of the time (McConnell, Kyl) and Senator Manchin

The Senate read it twice and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 308) on January 31, 2012 — the pre-printed 'Placed on Calendar' version suggests it was being teed up for floor action
That was the end of the line: the action history shows no committee markup, no floor debate, and no vote for the rest of the 112th Congress, which ended January 3, 2013

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the shortcut came out ahead: the State Department kept its authority over the cross-border permit, and the normal environmental review and court processes were left intact rather than overridden by statute for a single company.

for.name: John Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its push as sponsor, delivering introductory remarks on the Senate floor twice

for.name: 43 of 47 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Minority Leader Mitch McConnell and Whip Jon Kyl

for.name: 2 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democratic support it attracted

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote, despite its being placed on the calendar the day after introduction

against.name: Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Had denied the Keystone XL cross-border permit in January 2012 and opposed congressional legislation to override that decision

against.name: Environmental and landowner groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against fast-tracking the pipeline, focusing on spill risk and the Nebraska Sand Hills route

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican — 43 of the 47 Senate Republicans cosponsored versus 2 Democrats — and with Democratic leadership never scheduling a vote, the bill died along partisan lines without one.

industries.note: The bill would have handed one company statutory approval for its flagship project, plus exemption from the presidential permit, new environmental review, and multi-court litigation. The public got promised construction activity but lost the review process that vetted the route and safety conditions the bill itself leans on.

A direct, federally guaranteed route from Alberta to U.S. Gulf Coast markets would have locked in market access for tar sands crude. The counterweight is that the pipeline's climate and spill consequences fall on the public along the route.
Refiners configured to process heavy Canadian crude would gain a secure feedstock supply, with savings passed to consumers only indirectly at best.
